newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus parliament opposes hardline president. [CORRECTED 17:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Belarus parliament opposes hardline president. [CORRECTED 17:40 GMT]

text.p: Hardline Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko said on Friday that he intended to rule the former Soviet republic for 10 more years, but his recently united opponents ignored him and proposed eliminating his job.

Lukashenko, in an address to parliament, was promoting a new constitution extending his powers which he wants put to a referendum along with other issues on November 7, anniversary of the 1917 Bolshevik revolution.
"As regards your fears about prolonging my powers... Lukashenko will be president for a total of 12 years," he said.
After lengthy debate, deputies overwhelmingly approved a motion to put their own version of a constitution to a referendum -- doing away with the post of president.

"The president's constitution can in no way be described as democratic," Communist leader Sergei Kalyakin said. "Our version is truly democratic and does away with the post of president, which is not a traditional office for our society."
Deputies backed a November 25 (corrects from October) plebiscite, putting the president's and parliament's questions to voters in succession.
Lukashenko became Belarus's first post-Soviet president two years ago on a platform of fighting corruption and pressing for a union of some sort with neighbouring Russia.
Under his draft, the president may be elected for two five-year terms. Lukashenko's comments indicated he intended to start a full new mandate if the proposal wins approval.

The text calls for a new upper house of parliament, with a third of its members named by the president, who would be empowered to dissolve the assembly, call plebiscites and make appointments to the constitutional court and local government.
Lukashenko's rule has become increasingly authoritarian.
Up to 200 people have been given short jail terms for taking part in mass demonstrations last spring against his signing of a pact that would create a "community" with Russia.
On Thursday, seven extreme nationalists from Ukraine were given sentences of one to three years on more serious public order charges connected with the protests.
Two opposition politicians were granted political asylum in the United States in August after fleeing the country.

The president's has also cracked down on the press, with several editors sacked and a number of newspapers closed down or forced to publish abroad. An independent radio station in the capital Minsk was shut down last week by government order.

Lukashenko intends to put three other questions to a referendum to ban on private land ownership, entrench the death penalty and change the post-Soviet national holiday to honour the World War Two recapture of Minsk by Red Army troops.

Deputies sought two other referendum issues -- election of all regional officials and public controls on financing local government. Seven parties ranging from nationalists to liberals and communists agreed in July to bury differences to combat what they say is the threat of dictatorship under Lukashenko.
